questions.title: Who may legally give police entry consents under fourth amendment law?
questions.question_body:
In United States v.

Coleman, Mr.

Coleman argued that his wife never gave permission for Officer Kizer to enter their home even though she eventually opened her door after being asked twice.

I am confused about how third parties’ waivers are treated when neither has declared witness rights 

and yet were judged sufficient under United States v.

Banks 
and 

Schneckloth v.

Bustamonte – both cases show that a spouse may waive 

fourth amendment protections if she had legitimate expectation 

to privacy in her own home.

What precisely is required…?

questions.title: How do courts evaluate whether a consenting individual’s permission was voluntary?
questions.question_body:
"A problem arises when an officer asks repeatedly for permission," writes 

United States v.

Jones.

The opinion lists factors such as age,
intelligence,
education,
and whether counsel was advised during
the request.

In Coleman's trial,
eloaders recorded both an extended dialogue until motion “say she’d prefer you don’t” was made and >
three minutes passed before Officer Kizer re‑asked.

To me it isn’t clear how these operative clauses are applied when 
evidence is just
avid camera footage yet exists significant verbal flourish.

Could someone explain how *Bumper v North Carolina*’s *totality test* is applied “to determine *freely& voluntarily*?…
